1:
They agree on the date and differ on how much of the book this belongs to. Clarke puts it in Jehoiakim's reign, within the first three years; Ellicott makes it follow closely on the preceding chapter, a last warning whose rejection brings the same symbol back more decisively later. Gill treats it as a distinct prophecy connectable with what precedes, since it takes up the destruction threatened there. Keil and Delitzsch go wider and take three chapters as one compilation of two symbolical actions with their interpretation.

Where the potter worked is less certain. Gill says the house was well known to the prophet but its site is not; he reports the suggestion that Jeremiah was in the temple and the house lay beneath it, explaining the going down, and rejects it for a low-lying site outside the city near the potter's field. Ellicott identifies it with that field outright, notes that the traditional site lies on the southern face of the valley below the city, and adds that the soil is still a clay used for the same purpose. Then he raises the difficulty himself: buying the field to bury strangers implies waste ground whose use had been exhausted.

How the wheel worked they describe differently. Clarke reads the word as upon the stones and builds the machine accordingly: a moving stone turning on a fixed one below and carrying the surface where the vessel was made; the potter's wheel today, he says, is little different from the one in use three thousand years ago. Ellicott makes it two wheels: the potter sat driving a horizontal wheel with his feet while a smaller one turned under his hands.

Why the vessel was marred matters for the parable. Clarke offers a workshop answer — it did not stand in the working, or gravel worked into the mass made a breach, so the clay had to be kneaded afresh and put back on the wheel. Calvin fixes the moment: the vessel was spoiled while still soft in the potter's hand. Ellicott draws the consequence the others leave implicit — the marring is no fault of the potter but a defect in the material, and in application the resistance of the human agents God is fashioning; once marred, the potter may remould it to a less honourable use or, if hopeless, break it and begin again.

The application divides them along their schools. Gill and Calvin reach independently for one argument from the less to the greater: the potter did not make the clay he shapes, whereas God made the men he deals with, so his right over them is not merely as good as the potter's but better. Wesley grants the absolute power and bounds it at once — God acts as a just judge, rendering to every man according to his works. Ellicott states the boundary as a theory: the question implies a universe neither of fatalism crushing man's freedom nor of a sovereignty dissolved into man's choice, since the clay may resist the potter or yield willingly.

Clarke turns the same verse into a protest. He grants that the maker has a right to do with his creatures as reason and justice require, and to remake what does not answer. But he takes the apostle to have used the figure very differently, and puts a question of his own: would any potter make an exceedingly fair vessel on purpose to dash it to pieces when he had finished it? Surely not — and neither, he says, could the God of infinite perfection and love make millions of immortal souls on purpose for eternal perdition. Henry keeps to the errand rather than the doctrine: the prophet was sent not to preach a sermon but to receive one ready prepared, and those who would know God's mind must attend where his words are heard.
7:
The rule is stated twice, for threatening and for promise, and they differ on what kind of rule it is. Clarke makes it as general as it can be made: these verses contain what may be called the decree by which God's whole conduct towards man is regulated, so that a man under sentence who repents shall live and a man under promise who turns away shall die. Gill reads it the same way and extends it by name to Jews and Gentiles alike. Calvin agrees on the substance and then does what none of the others do — he marks the level at which the figure is used. This statement, he says, is the popular one, precisely because it turns on repentance; when the apostle took up the same similitude he did not speak so popularly but ascended higher, to what was in God's power to determine concerning every individual before the world was made.

Calvin fills out both halves where the others summarise. On the threatening side the point is to shut the mouths of men who would not be convinced their punishments were just: when God threatens ruin and the nation repents, he is reconciled at once. On the promising side he presses further — God does not merely pardon but is ready to load with every blessing those he had rejected as enemies; and the reverse holds, that he will tread in the dust the people he has favoured, if the favours are abused.

The application turns on a single word, and three of them catch it. Ellicott notes that the verb rendered frame is the one that describes the potter's work and gives the Hebrew its word for potter; Keil and Delitzsch say the same and add that the design in view is here an evil plot. Henry works the image out: God frames evil as the potter frames a vessel, so as to answer the end, and providence in all its operations is plainly working that way — look at your conduct and you cannot but see you deserve it.

Whether the vessel is already settled is the question underneath. Henry has the ruin in progress and the invitation offered so they may meet God in the way of his judgments and prevent his further proceedings. Ellicott holds the shape unfixed: this is the vessel in hand and its use is determined by its shape, but the form is not unalterable, and it is shown to frighten them into taking the warning. Calvin puts it as suspension rather than execution — vengeance prepared and hanging over their heads unless they turn in time.

Then comes the answer, and what kind of answer it is divides them. Ellicott hears defiance and not despair: better rendered as continued action, they say, not they said, the sense being that you need not hope we will do as you bid, for we go our own way. Keil and Delitzsch make the same grammatical point, that the form is of an action repeating itself in the present, and add that by this answer the prophet makes the people condemn themselves. Gill takes the hopelessness the other way — not that there was no hope of mercy on repentance, which has just been declared, but that they were so fixed that no room was left for the prophet to hope of reclaiming them. Calvin reports the usual rendering, that it is past hope, prefers it is all over, allows the verb may mean to be weary, and reads the whole as the obstinacy of men who thought they could secure themselves by joining now with the Assyrians and now with the Egyptians.

On the last word Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree against the English: what the people resolve to follow is not the imagination of the evil heart but its stubbornness.
13:
The heathen are called as witnesses. Ellicott renews the earlier appeal: Judah had not been true even as the nations were true to their inherited worship, and the virgin daughter is named to sharpen the contrast, fallen from a greater height to a lower depth. Calvin makes it a turning away in disgust — I will no more contend with brute animals, in whom there is no reason, but the Gentiles, though destitute of knowledge, can witness so gross an impiety. Clarke reports a variant: three manuscripts and the Alexandrian Greek read Jerusalem where the received text has Israel.

The snow of Lebanon then divides them four to one. Gill has the mountain named from its whiteness, like the Alps, its summer snow melting into streams that run down into the plain, and asks whether a thirsty traveller would pass such water untasted. Clarke puts it as a bargain: would any man in his senses abandon a farm always watered by those snows and take a barren rock? Wesley reduces it to a maxim, that reason teaches men not to forsake a greater good for a less. Calvin finds a twofold folly — running far for water when there is a spring in one's own field, and refusing pure cold water from afar because one would rather see the source. Ellicott stands against all four: the words a man are interpolated and pervert the verse, which should ask whether the snow of Lebanon fails from the rock or the cold streams from afar are dried up. The questions expect a no, and what is unfailing is the strength of God, which men forsook.

Calvin illustrates from his own doorstep: if a man today would not drink the river flowing past him but set off to taste the spring, everyone would laugh at the madness.

Who did the leading astray is not stated, and Ellicott supplies it: no persons are named, but the prophet plainly means the prophets and teachers who misled the people. He corrects the English twice more — the preposition from is not in the Hebrew, and the ancient paths, literally the paths of the age, stand in apposition to their ways and point to the immemorial faith. Wesley names that faith by its walkers, the way of Noah and Abraham and Jacob. On the vanity they burned incense to, Ellicott notes the word is not the one usually so rendered but the one used elsewhere of idols, where Keil and Delitzsch take it as the idols themselves.

How the passers-by react is a real disagreement. Clarke makes the hissing a shrieking, an expression of contempt. Ellicott denies it: the Hebrew is a sound-word for the inarticulate noise we make at something that makes us shudder, and the head-shaking is not the verb used elsewhere for scorn but one describing pity, so men would not mock the desolation but gaze at it astounded. Calvin catches a wordplay the others pass: the term for perpetual is the one just used of the ancient paths, there looking backward and here forward, so a people who alienated themselves from the ways of ages become a hissing of ages.

The east wind closes the passage. Clarke gives its character — it parches and blasts grain and trees, and cattle and men suffer — and quotes the old rhyme that when the wind blows from the east it is good for neither man nor beast. Wesley calls it the fiercest wind there. Ellicott reports that manuscripts vary between with and as an east wind without much affecting the sense, and turns to the second clause, where the figure is boldly anthropomorphic: the light of God's countenance is fulness of joy, and turning it away leaves them in the dark, a just return on a people who had turned him their back. Calvin argues that a comparison is intended whichever particle is read.
18:
The plot is answered in kind, and the conspirators' confidence examined. Ellicott takes their appeal to law, counsel and word as two claims: that they had guidance enough in the Law, the priests, and prophets who told them what they wished, and that it would continue whatever the threats. Wesley puts the boast more bluntly — we have the church on our side, and the regular priests and prophets know God's mind as well as he. Henry generalises it into the method of persecutors: they laid their heads together both to be revenged and to stop his mouth, and what enemies of religion cannot do separately they try in concert. He and Ellicott reach for the same parallel, the priests and elders taking counsel against Christ.

What they meant to do is disputed. Gill and Wesley keep it to speech — stopping his mouth, representing him as the thing the people hate. Clarke reads the preposition differently and gets a punishment rather than a slander: it should be rendered smite him on the tongue, and false testimony is punished in eastern countries to this day by striking the mouth with a strong piece of leather like a shoe sole, sometimes by running a bodkin through the tongue.

The prophet's turn to God is read as a rejoinder. Ellicott hears the exact answer to their resolve — they had said let us not give heed, and he says give heed to me. Gill draws the comfort out: God attends to his ministers' cries when men will not attend to their doctrine. Calvin makes the turn rhetorical: he could have reproved them to their faces, but it betokens more vehemence to leave men and address God.

What he claims for himself is disputed at a phrase. Clarke reads standing before God as intercession and says he was their continual intercessor; Ellicott takes it in its commoner sense of worship and communion with God. On the pit Ellicott recovers a vividness familiarity has worn away: the man was treated as a beast, the prophet who sought their good hunted like the wolf they trapped and killed. Calvin weighs the two sins — impiety is the more detestable, since God is above all mortals, but inhumanity has more baseness, being grosser and more evident, and men who hide their perfidy show it as soon as they deal with men.

Then come the curses, and every voice that touches them handles them differently. Clarke will not have them prayers at all: the execrations are simply prophetic declarations of judgments God was about to pour out, and are no directions to us, whose Lawgiver said love your enemies. Wesley asks the question outright and answers against the practice — it is not lawful for Christians to pray for evil against their enemies, and it is our duty to pray for the conversion of the worst of them. Calvin concedes more and defends more: the prophet seems driven by indignation into imprecations not consistent with a right feeling, and ought not to have uttered them, since God's children are to bear all injuries; but he was moved by the Holy Spirit, and what the Spirit dictates is not to be condemned. Ellicott declines the question. The words startle and pain us like the imprecations of the psalms, and how far they were righteous indignation not yet taught patience, and how far vindictiveness, we are not called on to inquire and could not decide; it is not ours to judge another man's servant, and righteous anger is at least a step towards righteous love.

The last verse draws two smaller notes. Keil and Delitzsch call it the summing up of the prayer and prefer the written text, and let them be cast down before thee, to the marginal that they may be. Ellicott objects to a supplied word: the thus inserted to emphasise the prayer weakens it.
